statement: Let $R>0$ and let $f\not\equiv 0$ be [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disc $|z-c|\le R$, with leading Laurent term $a(z-c)^m$ at $c$. Then the [circle average](c:circle-average) of $\log|f|$ over $|z-c|=R$ equals $\log|a| + m\log R + \sum_{u\ne c}\operatorname{ord}_u(f)\log\frac{R}{|u-c|}$, summed over the zeros and poles $u$ in the disc.

hypotheses.text: The radius satisfies $R>0$.
The function $f$ is [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) at every point of the closed disc $|z-c|\le R$.
The function $f$ is not identically zero.

conclusion: The [circle average](c:circle-average) of $\log|f|$ over $|z-c|=R$ equals $\log|a| + m\log R + \sum_{u\ne c}\operatorname{ord}_u(f)\log\frac{R}{|u-c|}$, where $\operatorname{ord}_u(f)$ is the order of $f$ at $u$, negative at a pole.

formal.difference: The declaration allows a radius of either sign, writes the zeros and poles as a divisor on the closed ball, and also covers $f\equiv 0$ by the convention $\log 0=0$. This statement assumes $R>0$ and $f\not\equiv 0$, and writes the divisor as orders.

proofs.name: Factor out zeros and poles
proofs.slogan: Divide out the zeros and poles of $f$, then average the logarithm of each factor around the circle.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The closed disc is compact, so $f$ has finitely many zeros and poles in it and every sum is finite.

roles.why: A positive radius gives a true circle, and $\log R$ is defined.
Meromorphy at each point of the compact disc gives finitely many zeros and poles and the factorization.
A function that is not identically zero has finite order at every point of the connected disc, so $a\ne0$ exists.

steps.slogan: Factor $f$ into a nonvanishing holomorphic function and its zeros and poles.
steps.detail: The closed disc is compact and $f\not\equiv0$, so $f$ has finitely many zeros and poles $u$ in it. Off a finite set, $f(z)=g(z)\prod_u(z-u)^{\operatorname{ord}_u(f)}$, with $g$ holomorphic and without zeros on a neighborhood of the disc.

steps.slogan: Split $\log|f|$ on the circle into a finite sum and $\log|g|$.
steps.detail: Off a finite set, $\log|f(z)|=\sum_u\operatorname{ord}_u(f)\log|z-u|+\log|g(z)|$. A finite set does not change a circle average, and averages add, so the average of $\log|f|$ is the sum of the two averages.

steps.slogan: Compute the circle average of $\log|z-u|$ for each zero or pole $u$.
steps.detail: For $|u-c|<R$ write $\log|z-u|=\log R+\log|1-w|$ with $w=(u-c)/(z-c)$. The function $\log|1-w|$ is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) on $|w|<1$ and vanishes at $0$, so its average is $0$ and the average is $\log R$; the case $|u-c|=R$ is a limit.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the average of $\log|g|$ by the mean value property.
steps.detail: Near the closed disc, $g$ has no zero, so $\log g$ is holomorphic on a slightly larger disc. The mean value property gives $\log g(c)$ as the average of $\log g$ on the circle; taking real parts, the average of $\log|g|$ is $\log|g(c)|$.

steps.slogan: Relate $\log|g(c)|$ to the leading coefficient $a$ of $f$ at $c$.
steps.detail: Compare the leading terms of the [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) at $c$ in the factorization. This gives $a=g(c)\prod_{u\ne c}(c-u)^{\operatorname{ord}_u(f)}$, so $\log|g(c)|=\log|a|-\sum_{u\ne c}\operatorname{ord}_u(f)\log|c-u|$.

steps.slogan: Add the averages and group the term at $c$ with the other terms.
steps.detail: The averages add to $\sum_u\operatorname{ord}_u(f)\log R+\log|a|-\sum_{u\ne c}\operatorname{ord}_u(f)\log|c-u|$. The term $u=c$ is $m\log R$, and each term $u\ne c$ becomes $\operatorname{ord}_u(f)\log\frac{R}{|u-c|}$, which is the formula.

concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The hypothesis gives the finite factorization into zeros and poles.
concepts.c:circle-average: Both sides of the formula are circle averages computed term by term.
concepts.c:harmonic-function: The function $\log|1-w|$ is harmonic, so its circle average is its center value.
concepts.c:laurent-series: The leading Laurent term at $c$ defines $m$ and $a$.

statement: Let $S\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty set of [diameter](c:diameter) $d<\infty$. Then $S$ lies in a closed ball of radius $d\sqrt{\frac{n}{2(n+1)}}$, that is, in an [enclosing ball](c:enclosing-ball) of that radius.

hypotheses.text: The set $S$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$.
The [diameter](c:diameter) of $S$ is $d<\infty$, so $|p-q|\le d$ for all $p,q\in S$.

conclusion: Some point $x\in\mathbb R^n$ has $|p-x|\le r$ for every $p\in S$, where $r=d\sqrt{n/(2(n+1))}$.

proofs.name: Minimal balls and Helly
proofs.slogan: Any $n+1$ points of $S$ lie in a ball of radius $r$ by a weighted distance count, and Helly's theorem then gives one ball for all of $S$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for bounded $S$ finite or infinite. The regular simplex shows that the radius is sharp.

roles.why: A nonempty set supplies the points whose balls Helly's theorem intersects.
Every pair of points is at distance at most $d$, which bounds the weighted sum of squared distances.

steps.slogan: Show that the center of a minimal enclosing ball lies in the hull of its contact points.
steps.detail: Let $P$ be finite and $B(x,\rho)$ the smallest closed ball containing it, with contact set $Q=\{p\in P:|p-x|=\rho\}$. If $x\notin\operatorname{conv}Q$, separate $x$ from the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) by a hyperplane and move $x$ slightly toward it. This shortens every distance to $Q$ and keeps the others below $\rho$, against minimality.

steps.slogan: Write the center as a convex combination of at most $n+1$ contact points.
steps.detail: By Carathéodory's theorem, $x=\sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_iq_i$ with $q_i\in Q$, $\lambda_i>0$, $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$ and $k\le n$. Translate so that $x=0$. Then $|q_i|=\rho$ and $\sum_i\lambda_iq_i=0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the weighted sum of squared distances between the contact points.
steps.detail: For each $j$, $\sum_i\lambda_i|q_i-q_j|^2=\sum_i\lambda_i(2\rho^2-2\langle q_i,q_j\rangle)=2\rho^2$, because $\sum_i\lambda_iq_i=0$. Multiplying by $\lambda_j$ and summing over $j$ gives $\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_j|q_i-q_j|^2=2\rho^2$.

steps.slogan: Bound that sum by the diameter to get $\rho\le r$.
steps.detail: Each $|q_i-q_j|\le d$ in the [diameter](c:diameter) bound, and the diagonal terms vanish, so $2\rho^2\le d^2\sum_{i\ne j}\lambda_i\lambda_j=d^2(1-\sum_i\lambda_i^2)$. By Cauchy-Schwarz, $\sum_i\lambda_i^2\ge\frac1{k+1}\ge\frac1{n+1}$, so $2\rho^2\le d^2\frac{n}{n+1}$.

steps.slogan: Intersect the balls of radius $r$ around the points of $S$ with Helly's theorem.
steps.detail: Any $n+1$ points of $S$ have a minimal ball of radius at most $r$, and its center lies in all $n+1$ balls $B(p,r)$. These balls are compact and convex, so Helly's theorem gives a point $x$ in all of them. Then $|p-x|\le r$ for every $p\in S$, so $B(x,r)$ is an [enclosing ball](c:enclosing-ball).

concepts.c:diameter: The diameter bounds every pairwise distance in the weighted sum.
concepts.c:enclosing-ball: The minimal balls and the final ball are enclosing balls of points of $S$.
concepts.c:convex-hull: The center of the minimal ball lies in the convex hull of its contact points.

source.note: The Helly route of Danzer, Grunbaum and Klee, Helly's theorem and its relatives (1963).

statement: Let a [crease pattern](c:crease-pattern) have $2n$ creases at one vertex inside a flat sheet, with consecutive [angles](c:angle) $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{2n}>0$ that sum to $2\pi$. The pattern folds flat if and only if $\alpha_1-\alpha_2+\alpha_3-\dots-\alpha_{2n}=0$.

hypotheses.text: The creases meet at one interior point of a flat sheet and cut it into sectors with [angles](c:angle) $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{2n}>0$ in cyclic order, with sum $2\pi$.
The number of creases is even, $2n$ with $n\ge1$.

conclusion: The pattern folds flat exactly when the alternating sum $\alpha_1-\alpha_2+\dots-\alpha_{2n}$ is zero.

proofs.name: Smallest angle induction
proofs.slogan: Necessity follows by tracking directions around the folded vertex, and sufficiency follows by induction that tucks the smallest sector between its neighbors.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence. An odd number of creases never folds flat, because every crease reverses the orientation of the paper.

roles.why: The positive angles sum to $2\pi$, which confines the alternating sum to an interval that holds one multiple of $2\pi$.
An even number of orientation flips closes the loop around the vertex, and the induction removes two creases at a time.

steps.slogan: Follow the image directions of the creases once around the folded vertex.
steps.detail: In a flat folding, each sector keeps its angle and neighboring sectors lie on the same side of their common crease. So the image direction turns by $+\alpha_1,-\alpha_2,+\alpha_3,\dots$ in turn. After one circuit it returns to its start, so $\sum_i(-1)^{i+1}\alpha_i\equiv0$ modulo $2\pi$.

steps.slogan: Show that the alternating sum lies strictly between $-2\pi$ and $2\pi$.
steps.detail: The odd-indexed angles sum to $A>0$ and the even-indexed angles sum to $B>0$, with $A+B=2\pi$. The alternating sum $A-B$ lies in $(-2\pi,2\pi)$ and is a multiple of $2\pi$, so it is $0$.

steps.slogan: For sufficiency, induct on $n$ and pick a smallest angle $\alpha_i$.
steps.detail: For $n=1$, the sum $\alpha_1-\alpha_2=0$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=2\pi$ gives $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\pi$, one straight crease, which folds flat. For $n\ge2$, let $\alpha_i$ be a smallest angle, so $\alpha_i\le\alpha_{i-1}$ and $\alpha_i\le\alpha_{i+1}$.

steps.slogan: Fold the two creases of the smallest sector to tuck it between its neighbors.
steps.detail: Fold sector $i$ over sector $i-1$, then fold sector $i+1$ back over sector $i$. Because $\alpha_i$ is at most both neighbors, sector $i$ lies inside both, and the three sectors form a Z-shaped stack of net width $\alpha_{i-1}-\alpha_i+\alpha_{i+1}$.

steps.slogan: Replace the three sectors by one sector and use the induction hypothesis.
steps.detail: The new vertex has $2n-2$ creases and the positive angle $\alpha_{i-1}-\alpha_i+\alpha_{i+1}$ in place of three. The angle sum and the alternating sum $0$ do not change, so the new pattern folds flat by induction. Replacing its merged sheet by the Z-shaped stack folds the original pattern flat.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: A flat folding forces the alternating sum to vanish, by the first two steps. Conversely, a zero alternating sum gives a flat folding, by the induction. So the pattern folds flat exactly when the alternating sum is zero.

concepts.c:crease-pattern: The theorem decides which single-vertex crease patterns fold flat.
concepts.c:angle: The sector angles and their alternating sum decide flat-foldability.

source.note: The textbook argument for the Kawasaki-Justin theorem, as in T. Hull, Project Origami, and Demaine and O'Rourke, Geometric Folding Algorithms.

statement: Let $f(z)=f_1z+f_2z^2+\cdots$ be analytic near $0$ with $f_1\ne0$, and let $g(w)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_nw^n$ be the [power series](c:power-series) of its local inverse, $g(f(z))=z$. Then $b_n=\frac1n[z^{n-1}]\bigl(z/f(z)\bigr)^n$ for every $n\ge1$, where $[z^k]h$ is the coefficient of $z^k$ in $h$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is analytic near $0$ with $f(0)=0$.
The derivative satisfies $f'(0)=f_1\ne0$, so $f$ has an analytic [inverse function](c:inverse-function) $g$ near $0$.

conclusion: For each $n\ge1$, $b_n=\frac1n[z^{n-1}](z/f(z))^n$, which equals $\frac1n\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}f(z)^{-n}$, the [residue](c:residue) of $f^{-n}$ at $0$.

proofs.name: Residue integral
proofs.slogan: Write $b_n$ as a contour integral, change the variable to $w=f(z)$, and integrate by parts to a residue at $0$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for each $n\ge1$. The inverse $g$ exists and is analytic near $0$ by the inverse function theorem.

roles.why: Analyticity of $f$ makes $f^{-n}$ meromorphic near $0$ with its only pole at $0$, so the residue is defined.
The condition $f'(0)\ne0$ gives the analytic inverse $g$ and makes $f$ conformal, so a small circle maps to a loop winding once around $0$.

steps.slogan: Write $b_n$ as a Cauchy integral of $g$ over a small circle.
steps.detail: The function $g$ is analytic near $0$, so for small $\varepsilon$ the coefficient formula of Cauchy's integral formula gives $b_n=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|w|=\varepsilon}\frac{g(w)}{w^{n+1}}\,dw$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $w=f(z)$ along a loop around $0$.
steps.detail: As $f'(0)\ne0$, the map $f$ sends a small circle $\gamma$ around $0$ one to one onto a loop winding once around $0$. With $g(f(z))=z$ and $dw=f'(z)\,dz$, $b_n=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{z\,f'(z)}{f(z)^{n+1}}\,dz$.

steps.slogan: Integrate by parts to remove the factor $z$.
steps.detail: Since $\frac{d}{dz}\bigl(-\frac{1}{n f^n}\bigr)=\frac{f'}{f^{n+1}}$, integration by parts gives $\oint_\gamma\frac{zf'}{f^{n+1}}dz=\bigl[-\frac{z}{nf^n}\bigr]_\gamma+\frac1n\oint_\gamma\frac{dz}{f^n}$. The bracket vanishes, because $z/f^n$ is single valued on the closed loop.

steps.slogan: Read the remaining integral as a residue at $0$.
steps.detail: So $b_n=\frac1n\cdot\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma f(z)^{-n}\,dz=\frac1n\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}f(z)^{-n}$, by the [residue](c:residue) theorem, since $0$ is the only pole inside $\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Convert the residue into a coefficient of $(z/f)^n$.
steps.detail: Write $f(z)^{-n}=z^{-n}(z/f(z))^n$, where $z/f(z)$ is analytic at $0$. The residue of $f^{-n}$ is then the coefficient of $z^{n-1}$ in $(z/f(z))^n$, so $b_n=\frac1n[z^{n-1}](z/f(z))^n$.

concepts.c:power-series: The coefficients $b_n$ of the inverse series are the quantities computed.
concepts.c:inverse-function: The inverse $g$ is the function whose Taylor coefficients are found.
concepts.c:residue: The coefficient of $w^n$ in $g$ becomes a residue at $0$.

source.note: The standard residue proof of the Lagrange-Burmann formula, as in Whittaker and Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis.

statement: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring), and let $I$ be a set of $k$ rows with $1\le k<n$. Let $A_{I,J}$ be the submatrix with rows $I$ and columns $J$, and let $I^c,J^c$ be the complements. Then $\det A=\sum_{|J|=k}(-1)^{\Sigma I+\Sigma J}\det A_{I,J}\det A_{I^c,J^c}$, where $\Sigma I$ is the sum of the elements of $I$.

hypotheses.text: The entries of $A$ lie in a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring).
The matrix $A$ is square, $n\times n$, and its [determinant](c:determinant) is the Leibniz sum over [permutations](c:permutation).
The row set $I$ has $k$ elements, with $1\le k<n$.

conclusion: The [determinant](c:determinant) equals $\sum_{|J|=k}(-1)^{\Sigma I+\Sigma J}\det A_{I,J}\det A_{I^c,J^c}$; for $k=1$ this is the expansion along one row.

proofs.name: Grouping the Leibniz sum
proofs.slogan: Group the terms of the Leibniz sum by the column set $J=\sigma(I)$, and factor each group into two determinants.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the case $k=1$ is the cofactor expansion along row $i$. The proof uses only commutativity of the ring.

roles.why: Commutativity lets the entries of each Leibniz term be regrouped into two products.
A square matrix has its determinant given by the Leibniz sum over $S_n$.
The set $I$ fixes the rows that split off, and $k<n$ keeps both complementary blocks nonempty.

steps.slogan: Write the determinant as the Leibniz sum over all permutations.
steps.detail: By definition $\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^na_{i,\sigma(i)}$. Each term picks one entry from every row and every column.

steps.slogan: Group the permutations by the column set $J=\sigma(I)$.
steps.detail: For each $k$-set $J$, the permutations $\sigma$ with $\sigma(I)=J$ correspond one to one to pairs of bijections $I\to J$ and $I^c\to J^c$. Every permutation lies in exactly one group.

steps.slogan: Compute the sign of $\sigma$ from signs on the two blocks.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma_0$ map $I$ onto $J$ and $I^c$ onto $J^c$, each in increasing order. Counting inversions gives $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma_0=(-1)^{\Sigma I+\Sigma J}$. Then $\sigma=\sigma_0\pi$ where $\pi$ permutes $I$ and $I^c$ separately, so $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma=(-1)^{\Sigma I+\Sigma J}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi|_I)\operatorname{sgn}(\pi|_{I^c})$.

steps.slogan: Split the sum of each group into a product of two determinants.
steps.detail: In the group of $J$, each term is $(-1)^{\Sigma I+\Sigma J}$ times $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi|_I)\prod_{i\in I}a_{i,\sigma(i)}$ times $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi|_{I^c})\prod_{i\notin I}a_{i,\sigma(i)}$. Summing over $\pi|_I$ and $\pi|_{I^c}$ independently gives $\det A_{I,J}\cdot\det A_{I^c,J^c}$, since the ring is commutative.

steps.slogan: Add the groups over all column sets $J$.
steps.detail: Summing the group results over all $k$-sets $J$ gives $\det A=\sum_{|J|=k}(-1)^{\Sigma I+\Sigma J}\det A_{I,J}\det A_{I^c,J^c}$. For $k=1$ and $I=\{i\}$ this is the expansion $\sum_j(-1)^{i+j}a_{ij}M_{ij}$ along row $i$.

concepts.c:determinant: The theorem expands the determinant, which the Leibniz sum defines.
concepts.c:commutative-ring: Commutativity lets entries be regrouped into two products.
concepts.c:permutation: Permutations index the Leibniz terms and carry their signs.
concepts.c:matrix: The square matrix $A$ is the object being expanded.

source.note: The standard proof from the Leibniz formula, as in the generalized Laplace expansion of the nLab page.

statement: Let $E$ be a real normed space and let $f\colon\mathbb C\to E$ be a [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) on the whole plane with bounded range. Then $f$ is constant.

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon\mathbb C\to E$ is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) on all of $\mathbb C$.
The range of $f$ is a bounded subset of $E$.

proofs.name: Harmonic conjugate and exponential
proofs.slogan: Reduce to real values with a norming functional, build a holomorphic function with that real part, and apply Liouville's theorem to its exponential.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for values in a real normed space; the real-valued case carries the idea.

roles.why: Harmonicity of $f$ passes to $\ell\circ f$ and gives a holomorphic function with that real part on the simply connected plane.
A bound $|\ell\circ f|\le M$ bounds $|e^F|$ by $e^M$.

steps.slogan: Choose a norming functional to reduce to a real harmonic function.
steps.detail: Fix $z,w$. By the Hahn-Banach theorem there is a continuous linear $\ell\colon E\to\mathbb R$ with $\|\ell\|=1$ and $\ell(f(z)-f(w))=\|f(z)-f(w)\|$. Then $u=\ell\circ f$ is real valued, harmonic and bounded by some $M$.

steps.slogan: Find an entire function $F$ whose real part is $u$.
steps.detail: A real harmonic function on the simply connected plane has a harmonic conjugate. So there is an entire [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $F$ with $\operatorname{Re}F=u$.

steps.slogan: Form the entire function $e^F$ and bound its modulus.
steps.detail: The function $e^F$ is entire, and $|e^F|=e^{\operatorname{Re}F}=e^u\le e^M$. So $e^F$ is a bounded entire function.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $e^F$ is constant by Liouville's theorem.
steps.detail: Liouville's theorem says that a bounded entire function is constant. Hence $e^F$ is constant on $\mathbb C$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that $u$ is constant and that $f(z)=f(w)$.
steps.detail: A constant $e^F$ has constant modulus $e^u$, so $u$ is constant. Then $\|f(z)-f(w)\|=\ell(f(z)-f(w))=u(z)-u(w)=0$.

concepts.c:harmonic-function: The hypothesis is kept by the linear functional and gives the conjugate.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The conjugate gives a holomorphic function whose exponential is bounded.

statement: Let $\varphi$ be a scalar field with one stable particle of mass $m$, $\langle\Omega|\varphi|\Omega\rangle=0$ and $\langle p|\varphi(0)|\Omega\rangle=\sqrt Z$. Let $\tilde G$ be the Fourier transform of the vacuum [time-ordered product](c:time-ordered-product) of $n+k$ fields. As all external $p_j^2\to m^2$, $\prod_j\frac{p_j^2-m^2}{i\sqrt Z}\,\tilde G\to\langle p_1\dots p_n|S|q_1\dots q_k\rangle$, the connected [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) element.

hypotheses.text: The field $\varphi$ is a scalar field with one stable particle of mass $m$ and $\langle\Omega|\varphi|\Omega\rangle=0$.
The field obeys the asymptotic condition: smeared by a wave packet, it tends to $\sqrt Z$ times a free in field as $t\to-\infty$ and a free out field as $t\to+\infty$, with $Z>0$.

conclusion: Near the mass shell, $\tilde G$ has a simple pole $\frac{i\sqrt Z}{p_j^2-m^2}$ in each external momentum, and the residue is the connected [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) element.

proofs.name: Asymptotic fields and poles
proofs.slogan: Write the in and out particle operators as limits of the smeared field, then read each pole of the correlator from the late-time region of one field.
proofs.scope: A physical-level derivation for one scalar field with one stable particle species, as in the textbooks. The limits are taken from the asymptotic condition, which Haag-Ruelle scattering theory makes precise.

roles.why: The isolated one-particle states of mass $m$ are the intermediate states that produce the poles.
The asymptotic condition identifies the in and out operators with limits of the field, with factor $\sqrt Z$.

steps.slogan: Describe the external particles by in and out operators built from the field.
steps.detail: Let $A_p(t)=i\int d^3x\,e^{ip\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_0}\varphi(x)$, smeared by a wave packet. The asymptotic condition says that $A_p(t)$ tends to $\sqrt Z$ times the out operator of momentum $p$ as $t\to+\infty$, and to $\sqrt Z$ times the in operator as $t\to-\infty$. The [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) element is the overlap of an out state with an in state.

steps.slogan: Write the difference of the two limits as a spacetime integral of $(\Box+m^2)\varphi$.
steps.detail: Since $(\Box+m^2)e^{ip\cdot x}=0$ on shell, integration by parts in space gives $\partial_tA_p(t)=i\int d^3x\,e^{ip\cdot x}(\Box+m^2)\varphi(x)$, because wave packets kill the boundary terms. The fundamental theorem of calculus then gives $A_p(+\infty)-A_p(-\infty)=i\int d^4x\,e^{ip\cdot x}(\Box+m^2)\varphi(x)$.

steps.slogan: Isolate the pole of one field insertion from its late-time region.
steps.detail: Take $x^0$ later than all other times, so $T\varphi(x)\mathcal O=\varphi(x)\,T\mathcal O$. A complete set of states gives $\langle\Omega|\varphi(x)|\mathbf k\rangle=\sqrt Z\,e^{-ik\cdot x}$ for one-particle states, and the late $x^0$ integral gives $\frac{i}{p^0-E_{\mathbf p}+i\epsilon}$. This is a pole at the mass shell with weight $i\sqrt Z$, and by step 2 the factor $(\Box+m^2)$ cancels it.

steps.slogan: Repeat for every external particle and identify the result with the S-matrix element.
steps.detail: Treat each outgoing momentum at late times and each incoming momentum at early times. Each step strips one field, contributes $\frac{i\sqrt Z}{p_j^2-m^2+i\epsilon}$ and leaves that particle as an external state. What remains is the overlap of out and in states, $\langle p_1\dots p_n|S|q_1\dots q_k\rangle$, which gives the formula.

concepts.c:s-matrix: The theorem expresses S-matrix elements through correlation functions.
concepts.c:time-ordered-product: The correlator is a vacuum expectation of a time-ordered product.

source.note: The textbook derivation of Peskin and Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory, section 7.2; the formula is from Lehmann, Symanzik and Zimmermann, Nuovo Cimento 1 (1955).

statement: For two candidates and $n\ge1$ voters, a ballot is $+1$ (prefers $A$), $0$ (indifferent) or $-1$ (prefers $B$). Majority rule $v\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}\sum_iv_i$ is anonymous, neutral and positively responsive. Conversely, every [social choice function](c:social-choice-function) with these three properties is [majority rule](c:majority-rule).

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon\{-1,0,1\}^n\to\{-1,0,1\}$ is a [social choice function](c:social-choice-function) for $n\ge1$ voters.
The rule $f$ is anonymous: $f(v\circ\pi)=f(v)$ for every permutation $\pi$ of the voters.
The rule $f$ is neutral: $f(-v)=-f(v)$ for every profile $v$.
The rule $f$ is positively responsive: if $f(v)\ge0$ and one voter raises their ballot, giving $v'$, then $f(v')=+1$.

conclusion: $f(v)=\operatorname{sgn}\sum_iv_i$ for every profile $v$, so $f$ is [majority rule](c:majority-rule); and majority rule has the three properties.

proofs.name: Tie lifting
proofs.slogan: Anonymity and neutrality force a tie to give $0$, and positive responsiveness lifts a tie to a win for the side with more votes.
proofs.scope: All profiles with $n\ge1$ voters. A profile with more $-1$ than $+1$ ballots follows from the mirror case by neutrality.

roles.why: Three ballot values and three outcomes make $\operatorname{sgn}\sum v_i$ a valid outcome of the same kind.
Permuting voters shows that a tied profile has the same outcome as its mirror image.
Reversing every ballot reverses the outcome, which forces ties to give $0$ and mirrors the lifting step.
Raising one ballot from a tie outcome gives $+1$, and raising more ballots keeps $+1$.

steps.slogan: Show that every tied profile has outcome $0$.
steps.detail: Let $v$ have as many $+1$ ballots as $-1$ ballots. Then $-v$ is a permutation of $v$, so $f(-v)=f(v)$ by anonymity. Neutrality gives $f(-v)=-f(v)$, so $f(v)=-f(v)$ and $f(v)=0$.

steps.slogan: Lift a profile with more $+1$ ballots from a tie by raising ballots.
steps.detail: Let $v$ have $d>0$ more $+1$ ballots than $-1$ ballots. Lower $d$ of the $+1$ ballots to $0$ to get a tied profile $w$, with $f(w)=0$. Raise these ballots back one at a time: the first raise gives $+1$ by positive responsiveness, and each later raise keeps $+1$, since $+1\ge0$. So $f(v)=+1$.

steps.slogan: Mirror the profile to treat the case of more $-1$ ballots.
steps.detail: Let $v$ have more $-1$ ballots than $+1$ ballots. Then $-v$ has more $+1$ ballots, so $f(-v)=+1$ by the lifting step. Neutrality gives $f(v)=-1$.

steps.slogan: Check that majority rule has the three properties.
steps.detail: The map $v\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}\sum_iv_i$ ignores the order of the voters, and $\operatorname{sgn}\sum_i(-v_i)=-\operatorname{sgn}\sum_iv_i$. If $\sum_iv_i\ge0$ and one ballot rises by at least $1$, the sum becomes at least $1$, so the outcome is $+1$.

steps.slogan: Combine the three cases of the count into the formula.
steps.detail: Every profile has more $+1$ ballots, more $-1$ ballots, or a tie, and the outcomes $+1$, $-1$, $0$ match $\operatorname{sgn}\sum_iv_i$. So $f$ is majority rule, and by the converse step majority rule has the three properties.

concepts.c:social-choice-function: The theorem characterizes this kind of map from ballots to outcomes.
concepts.c:majority-rule: Majority rule is the rule that the three properties single out.

source.note: A short proof in the spirit of K. O. May, A set of independent necessary and sufficient conditions for simple majority decision, Econometrica 20 (1952).

statement: Let $R>0$. Let $f$ be complex differentiable on the open disc $|z-c|<R$ and continuous on its closure, with values in $\mathbb C$ or a complex Banach space. Then the [circle average](c:circle-average) $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(c+Re^{i\theta})\,d\theta$ equals $f(c)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is complex differentiable on the open disc $|z-c|<R$, so it is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) there.
The function $f$ is continuous on the closed disc $|z-c|\le R$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes values in a complex Banach space and allows a radius of either sign, using $|R|$. The case $R=0$ is trivial there, as the average over a point is the value.

proofs.name: Cauchy integral at the center
proofs.slogan: Write $f(c)$ with Cauchy's integral formula on the circle, then turn the contour integral into a circle average.
proofs.scope: The case $R>0$. For $R=0$ the circle is the point $c$ and the average is $f(c)$.

roles.why: Holomorphy inside the circle makes Cauchy's integral formula valid.
Continuity up to the circle makes the boundary integral defined and the formula valid on the closed disc.

steps.slogan: Write $f(c)$ as a Cauchy integral over the circle.
steps.detail: For $R>0$, Cauchy's integral formula, in the form for $f$ continuous on the closed disc and holomorphic inside, gives $f(c)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-c|=R}\frac{f(z)}{z-c}\,dz$.

steps.slogan: Parametrize the circle by $z=c+Re^{i\theta}$.
steps.detail: Then $dz=iRe^{i\theta}\,d\theta=i(z-c)\,d\theta$, so $\frac{dz}{z-c}=i\,d\theta$ along the circle. Hence the contour integral becomes $f(c)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}f(c+Re^{i\theta})\,i\,d\theta$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the factor $i$ to get the circle average.
steps.detail: The factors $\frac1{2\pi i}$ and $i$ combine to $\frac1{2\pi}$. So $f(c)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(c+Re^{i\theta})\,d\theta$, the [circle average](c:circle-average) of $f$.

concepts.c:circle-average: The conclusion identifies $f(c)$ with the circle average of $f$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy inside the disc makes Cauchy's formula available.

source.note: mathlib specializes DiffContOnCl.circleAverage_smul_div, the Cauchy formula for circle averages, to w = c, where (z - c)/(z - c) = 1 on the circle.

statement: Let $X$ be a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) Hausdorff space and $Y$ a [Banach space](c:banach-space). Let $F$ assign to each $x\in X$ a nonempty closed [convex](c:convex-set) set $F(x)\subseteq Y$, and let $F$ be [lower hemicontinuous](c:lower-hemicontinuous-map). Then there is a continuous $g\colon X\to Y$ with $g(x)\in F(x)$ for every $x$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) Hausdorff space.
The space $Y$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space).
Each value $F(x)$ is nonempty, closed and [convex](c:convex-set).
The map $F$ is [lower hemicontinuous](c:lower-hemicontinuous-map): for each open $U\subseteq Y$, the set $\{x:F(x)\cap U\ne\emptyset\}$ is open.

conclusion: There is a continuous map $g\colon X\to Y$ with $g(x)\in F(x)$ for every $x\in X$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows a normal paracompact domain and a complete first-countable locally convex real topological vector space as codomain, which includes every Banach space. This statement takes a paracompact Hausdorff domain, which is normal, and a Banach space.

proofs.name: Successive approximate selections
proofs.slogan: Build continuous maps that come within $2^{-n}$ of $F$ and within $2^{1-n}$ of each other, then pass to the uniform limit.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The neighborhoods $V_n$ of $0$ are the open balls of radius $2^{-n}$.

roles.why: Paracompactness gives locally finite partitions of unity, which glue local choices into continuous maps.
Completeness gives the limit of the uniformly Cauchy sequence, and balls are convex.
Convexity keeps averages of nearby choices near $F(x)$, and closedness puts the limit in $F(x)$.
Lower hemicontinuity makes the covering sets open, which is what the partition of unity needs.

steps.slogan: Build a continuous map $h_0$ with $h_0(x)\in F(x)+V_0$.
steps.detail: For $y\in Y$, the set $U_y=\{x:F(x)\cap(y+V_0)\ne\emptyset\}$ is open by lower hemicontinuity, and these sets cover $X$. Take a locally finite [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) $(\phi_y)$ subordinate to the cover and put $h_0(x)=\sum_y\phi_y(x)\,y$. Each $y$ with $\phi_y(x)>0$ lies in the convex set $F(x)+V_0$, so $h_0(x)\in F(x)+V_0$.

steps.slogan: Refine each map $h_n$ to a closer map $h_{n+1}$ that still approximates $F$.
steps.detail: The map $x\mapsto F(x)\cap(h_n(x)+V_n)$ has nonempty values, because $h_n(x)\in F(x)+V_n$, and it is lower hemicontinuous with convex values. Step 1 applied to it with radius $2^{-(n+1)}$ gives a continuous $h_{n+1}$ with $h_{n+1}(x)\in F(x)+V_{n+1}$ and $|h_{n+1}(x)-h_n(x)|<2^{1-n}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the sequence $(h_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy.
steps.detail: For $m>n$ and every $x$, $|h_m(x)-h_n(x)|<\sum_{j=n}^{m-1}2^{1-j}<2^{2-n}$. So the sequence is uniformly Cauchy on $X$.

steps.slogan: Take the uniform limit $g$ of $(h_n)$ and check that it is continuous.
steps.detail: Since $Y$ is complete, $h_n(x)$ converges for each $x$ to a point $g(x)$. A uniform limit of continuous maps is continuous, so $g$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Show that $g(x)$ lies in $F(x)$ by closedness.
steps.detail: The distance from $h_n(x)$ to $F(x)$ is less than $2^{-n}$, which tends to $0$. So $g(x)$ is at distance $0$ from $F(x)$, and $F(x)$ is closed, so $g(x)\in F(x)$.

concepts.c:paracompact-space: Paracompactness supplies the partitions of unity that glue local selections.
concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness lets the uniformly Cauchy sequence converge.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity keeps averages of nearby choices near the value of $F$.
concepts.c:lower-hemicontinuous-map: Lower hemicontinuity makes the covering sets open.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: The partition of unity averages local choices into one continuous map.

source.note: mathlib starts from HasOpenLowerSections.exists_continuous_selection, refines with exists_continuous_selection_refine, proves UniformCauchySeqOn, takes the limit with cauchySeq_tendsto_of_complete and uses closedness through the intersection of closures.

statement: Let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a full-rank [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) and $K$ a [convex body](c:convex-body) with $K=-K$. Let $\lambda_k$ be the least $\lambda>0$ such that $\lambda K$ contains $k$ linearly independent points of $\Lambda$. Then $\frac{2^n}{n!}\frac{\det\Lambda}{\operatorname{vol}K}\le\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n\le2^n\frac{\det\Lambda}{\operatorname{vol}K}$.

hypotheses.text: The set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of rank $n$.
The set $K$ is a [convex body](c:convex-body): compact, convex, with nonempty interior, and symmetric, $K=-K$.

proofs.name: Flag argument with Minkowski's first theorem
proofs.slogan: Choose independent lattice vectors that realize the minima, bound the volume below by a cross-polytope, and bound the product above by the cited argument built on Minkowski's first theorem.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proofs: the lower bound is proved in full, and the upper bound rests on the cited argument. The lattice has full rank in $\mathbb R^n$ and $K$ is a symmetric convex body.

roles.why: Discreteness of the lattice makes the minima attained, and its determinant is the unit of volume in both bounds.
Compactness attains the minima, and convexity with symmetry puts the cross-polytope inside $K$.

steps.slogan: Choose independent lattice vectors that realize the successive minima.
steps.detail: The body $K$ is compact and $\Lambda$ is discrete, so each minimum $\lambda_k$ is attained. There are linearly independent $b_1,\dots,b_n\in\Lambda$ with $b_k\in\lambda_k\partial K$, that is, with gauge value $\lambda_k$.

steps.slogan: Show that lattice vectors outside $\operatorname{span}(b_1,\dots,b_{k-1})$ lie outside the interior of $\lambda_kK$.
steps.detail: For $\lambda<\lambda_k$, the lattice points of $\lambda K$ span a space of dimension at most $k-1$, and $b_1,\dots,b_{k-1}$ already span a space of that dimension inside $\lambda K$. So every lattice vector outside $\operatorname{span}(b_1,\dots,b_{k-1})$ has gauge at least $\lambda_k$.

steps.slogan: Bound the volume of $K$ from below by a cross-polytope.
steps.detail: The points $\pm b_k/\lambda_k$ lie in $K$, so $K$ contains their convex hull, of volume $\frac{2^n}{n!\,\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n}|\det(b_1,\dots,b_n)|$. The determinant is a positive integer multiple of $\det\Lambda$, so $\operatorname{vol}K\ge\frac{2^n\det\Lambda}{n!\,\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n}$, which is the lower bound.

steps.slogan: Prove the upper bound by the cited argument that combines the flag property with Minkowski's first theorem.
steps.detail: This is the deep part. Minkowski's original proof, the proofs of Weyl and Davenport in Bambah, Woods and Zassenhaus, and Henk's account use the flag property of step 2 together with Minkowski's convex body theorem. The argument is lengthy and is not reproduced here.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds on the product of the minima.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n\ge\frac{2^n}{n!}\frac{\det\Lambda}{\operatorname{vol}K}$, and step 4 gives $\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n\le2^n\frac{\det\Lambda}{\operatorname{vol}K}$. Together they are the stated inequalities.

concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: The lattice supplies the independent vectors and the determinant.
concepts.c:convex-body: The cross-polytope lies inside the convex body, and volumes are compared.
concepts.c:successive-minima: The theorem bounds the product of the successive minima.

source.ref: M. Henk, Successive minima and lattice points, Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo, Serie II, Supplemento 70 (2002); classical proofs: R. P. Bambah, A. Woods and H. Zassenhaus, Three proofs of Minkowski's second inequality in the geometry of numbers, Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society 5 (1965), 453-462.
source.note: Henk presents Minkowski's own proof in modern language; the lower bound is the cross-polytope argument.

statement: Let $T$ be a complete first-order theory in a [countable language](c:countable-language) with an infinite model. If all models of $T$ of some uncountable [cardinality](c:cardinal-number) $\kappa$ are isomorphic, then all models of $T$ of every uncountable cardinality $\lambda$ are isomorphic.

hypotheses.text: The theory $T$ is complete, in a [countable language](c:countable-language), and has an infinite model.
The theory $T$ is $\kappa$-categorical for some uncountable [cardinal](c:cardinal-number) $\kappa$: any two models of cardinality $\kappa$ are isomorphic.

conclusion: The theory $T$ is $\lambda$-categorical for every uncountable cardinal $\lambda$.

proofs.name: Strongly minimal sets (Baldwin-Lachlan)
proofs.slogan: A theory categorical in one uncountable power is $\omega$-stable with no Vaughtian pair, so each model is determined by the dimension of a strongly minimal set.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof: every step rests on the cited work. The language is countable and the theory is complete with infinite models.

roles.why: Completeness and a countable language make the counting of types and the Morley rank available.
Categoricity in $\kappa$ rules out non-isomorphic models of size $\kappa$, which gives $\omega$-stability and no Vaughtian pair.

steps.slogan: Show that categoricity in an uncountable power makes $T$ $\omega$-stable.
steps.detail: If $T$ were not $\omega$-stable, some countable set would carry uncountably many types. One builds a model of size $\kappa$ realizing uncountably many of them, and an Ehrenfeucht-Mostowski model of size $\kappa$ realizing only countably many. These models are not isomorphic, against $\kappa$-categoricity (Morley 1965).

steps.slogan: Find a strongly minimal formula by Morley rank.
steps.detail: An $\omega$-stable theory has Morley rank, and a formula of least rank and degree $1$ defines a strongly minimal set $D$. In every model $M$, the algebraic closure on $D(M)$ is a pregeometry, so $D(M)$ has a dimension (Baldwin and Lachlan 1971).

steps.slogan: Show that $T$ has no Vaughtian pair.
steps.detail: A Vaughtian pair is a proper [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) $M\prec N$ with an infinite definable set having $\varphi(M)=\varphi(N)$. Such a pair would give, by the two-cardinal theorem and Lowenheim-Skolem arguments, models of size $\kappa$ with different dimensions of $D$, which are not isomorphic. So there is no Vaughtian pair.

steps.slogan: Show that every model is prime over its strongly minimal set.
steps.detail: With no Vaughtian pair, each model $M$ is prime over $D(M)$ together with the finitely many parameters that define $D$. So $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by the dimension of $D(M)$.

steps.slogan: Compute that dimension in every uncountable cardinality $\lambda$.
steps.detail: For a model $M$ of uncountable size $\lambda$, being prime over $D(M)$ gives $|M|=\max(|D(M)|,\aleph_0)$, so $D(M)$ has dimension $\lambda$. Two models of size $\lambda$ are prime over strongly minimal sets of equal dimension, hence isomorphic, so $T$ is $\lambda$-categorical.

concepts.c:countable-language: A countable language lets one count types over countable sets.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The theorem compares categoricity across different uncountable cardinalities.
concepts.c:elementary-embedding: A Vaughtian pair is a proper elementary extension that keeps one definable set.

source.ref: M. Morley, Categoricity in power, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 114 (1965), 514-538; strongly minimal route: J. T. Baldwin and A. H. Lachlan, On strongly minimal sets, Journal of Symbolic Logic 36 (1971), 79-96.
source.note: Morley proves omega-stability by Ehrenfeucht-Mostowski models; Baldwin and Lachlan give the strongly minimal proof that the steps follow.

statement: Let $X$ be a [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface) of genus at least $2$. A [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) of degree $0$ on $X$ is [stable](c:stable-bundle) if and only if it carries an irreducible unitary [flat connection](c:flat-connection) compatible with its holomorphic structure, equivalently comes from an irreducible [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation) of $\pi_1(X)$. The connection is unique up to unitary gauge.

hypotheses.text: The surface $X$ is a [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface) of genus $g\ge2$.
The bundle $E$ is a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) of rank $r$ and degree $0$ on $X$.

conclusion: The bundle $E$ is [stable](c:stable-bundle) if and only if it carries an irreducible unitary [flat connection](c:flat-connection) compatible with its holomorphic structure, and this connection is unique up to unitary gauge.

proofs.name: Gauge-theoretic proof (Donaldson)
proofs.slogan: A flat unitary bundle is stable by a curvature estimate, and a stable bundle carries a flat unitary metric found by a variational argument over Hermitian metrics.
proofs.scope: An outline of Donaldson's proof: the analytic existence steps rest on the cited paper. The genus assumption is that of the original theorem.

roles.why: On a Riemann surface, a Yang-Mills connection is projectively flat, so the minimizer is flat in degree $0$.
Degree $0$ makes flat connections possible, and the holomorphic structure defines the orbit of metrics that is searched.

steps.slogan: Show that a bundle with an irreducible flat unitary connection is stable.
steps.detail: For a holomorphic subbundle $F\subset E$, the Chern-Weil formula and the second fundamental form give $\deg F\le0$, with equality only when $F$ is parallel for the flat connection. Irreducibility excludes a proper parallel subbundle, so every proper $F$ has $\deg F<0$ and $E$ is [stable](c:stable-bundle) (Narasimhan and Seshadri 1965).

steps.slogan: Recast the converse as a search for a Hermitian metric with a flat Chern connection.
steps.detail: A unitary [flat connection](c:flat-connection) compatible with the holomorphic structure is the Chern connection of a Hermitian metric on $E$. So one looks for a metric of curvature zero in the complex gauge orbit of the holomorphic structure, which is a minimum of a Yang-Mills type functional.

steps.slogan: Minimize the functional over the orbit by induction on the rank.
steps.detail: Donaldson defines a functional on Hermitian metrics, essentially $\|F\|_{L^2}^2$ in rank $2$, and chooses it so that induction on the rank works. A minimizing sequence is controlled by elliptic estimates.

steps.slogan: Use stability to keep the minimizing sequence bounded.
steps.detail: If the gauge transformations along the sequence became unbounded, a rescaled limit would define a proper holomorphic subbundle of degree at least $0$, against stability. So the sequence converges, and the minimum is attained at a Yang-Mills connection.

steps.slogan: Show that the minimizer is flat and irreducible.
steps.detail: On a Riemann surface a Yang-Mills connection is projectively flat, and in degree $0$ it is flat. A reducible flat connection would split $E$ holomorphically into summands of degree $0$, against stability, so the connection is irreducible.

steps.slogan: Prove uniqueness up to unitary gauge by comparing two metrics.
steps.detail: Two flat unitary connections on the stable bundle $E$ give two Hermitian metrics, and their ratio is a holomorphic endomorphism of $E$. A stable bundle has only scalar endomorphisms, so the metrics agree up to a constant and the connections are unitarily gauge equivalent.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that an irreducible flat unitary connection makes $E$ stable. Steps 2 to 5 show that a stable $E$ carries such a connection, and step 6 shows that it is unique up to unitary gauge.

concepts.c:stable-bundle: Stability is the algebraic condition equivalent to a flat unitary connection.
concepts.c:flat-connection: The flat connection is what the theorem constructs and compares.
concepts.c:compact-riemann-surface: The base is a compact surface of genus at least two.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: The theorem classifies holomorphic bundles of degree zero.
concepts.c:unitary-representation: Irreducible unitary representations of the fundamental group give the flat bundles.

source.ref: S. K. Donaldson, A new proof of a theorem of Narasimhan and Seshadri, Journal of Differential Geometry 18 (1983), 269-277; original proof: M. S. Narasimhan and C. S. Seshadri, Stable and unitary vector bundles on a compact Riemann surface, Annals of Mathematics 82 (1965), 540-567.
source.note: The steps follow Donaldson's gauge-theoretic proof; the first step is the easy direction of Narasimhan and Seshadri.

statement: Every [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) closed [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) is homeomorphic to the $3$-sphere $S^3$.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a closed, connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold): compact, without boundary.
The manifold $M$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space): $\pi_1(M)=1$.

proofs.name: Ricci flow with surgery
proofs.slogan: Run Ricci flow with surgery on $M$, show that it dies out in finite time, and read the topology of $M$ from the surgeries.
proofs.scope: An outline of Perelman's proof as completed by Morgan and Tian: each step rests on the cited work. A topological $3$-manifold has a smooth structure by Moise's theorem, so the smooth case suffices.

roles.why: Compactness gives short-time existence of the flow and finitely many surgeries in finite time, and surgery stays within closed $3$-manifolds.
Trivial fundamental group gives finite extinction and rules out every non-simply-connected summand.

steps.slogan: Give $M$ a Riemannian metric and start the Ricci flow.
steps.detail: By Moise's theorem $M$ is smooth. Choose a metric $g_0$ and evolve it by the [Ricci flow](c:ricci-flow) $\partial_tg=-2\operatorname{Ric}(g)$, as Hamilton did. The flow exists for a short time and can develop singularities.

steps.slogan: Continue the flow through surgeries on necks for all time.
steps.detail: Perelman's entropy gives noncollapsing, and the classification of $\kappa$-solutions shows that regions of large curvature look like necks or caps. One cuts along small neck spheres, glues in balls, discards components of known topology and continues, with finitely many surgeries in each finite time.

steps.slogan: Show that the flow with surgery on a simply connected manifold ends in finite time.
steps.detail: Perelman, and later Colding and Minicozzi, show that when $\pi_1(M)$ is trivial the flow with surgery becomes extinct in finite time. The width of the family of maps that measures the homotopy of $M$ tends to zero.

steps.slogan: Reverse the surgeries to read off the topology of $M$.
steps.detail: Undoing a surgery is a connected sum, which adds an $S^2\times S^1$ summand when the sphere does not separate. So $M$ is a connected sum of the discarded components, each a quotient of $S^3$ or an $S^2\times S^1$ type piece. The group $\pi_1(M)$ is their free product and is trivial, so every summand is $S^3$ and $M\cong S^3$.

concepts.c:ricci-flow: The flow deforms the metric and its surgeries detect the topology.
concepts.c:3-manifold: The theorem and the surgery analysis both concern $3$-manifolds.
concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Trivial fundamental group gives finite extinction and removes the other summands.

source.ref: J. Morgan and G. Tian, Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture, Clay Mathematics Monographs 3, American Mathematical Society and Clay Mathematics Institute, 2007, expanding G. Perelman's three preprints on the Ricci flow (2002-2003).
source.note: Morgan and Tian give a complete proof; the finite extinction step is also due to Colding and Minicozzi.

statement: Let $f$ be a $C^1$ vector field on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, and let the forward orbit of $x$ for the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot y=f(y)$ stay in a compact set $K\subset U$. If the [limit set](c:limit-set) $\omega(x)$ contains no equilibrium, then $\omega(x)$ is a [periodic orbit](c:periodic-orbit).

hypotheses.text: The field $f$ is $C^1$ on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, so the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot y=f(y)$ has unique solutions.
The forward orbit of $x$ stays in a compact set $K\subset U$.
The [limit set](c:limit-set) $\omega(x)$ contains no equilibrium of $f$.

conclusion: The limit set $\omega(x)$ is a single [periodic orbit](c:periodic-orbit).

proofs.name: Transversal sections
proofs.slogan: A limit set without equilibria meets each transversal in one point, so one of its points has a closed orbit, and connectedness makes that orbit the whole limit set.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for the plane; the proof uses the Jordan curve theorem. The orbit of $x$ may itself be periodic, and then $\omega(x)$ is that orbit.

roles.why: Unique solutions make orbits disjoint curves and give flow boxes at regular points.
Compactness makes $\omega(x)$ nonempty, compact, connected and invariant.
Without equilibria, every point of $\omega(x)$ has a transversal section.

steps.slogan: Show that the limit set is nonempty, compact, connected and invariant.
steps.detail: The forward orbit lies in the compact set $K$, so $\omega(x)=\bigcap_T\overline{\{\phi_t(x):t\ge T\}}$ is a decreasing intersection of nonempty compact connected sets. It is invariant because each flow map $\phi_s$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Show that an orbit crosses a transversal segment in monotone order.
steps.detail: At a regular point $q$, a short segment $L$ transverse to $f$ is crossed by nearby orbits inside a flow box. By the [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve) theorem, an orbit meets $L$ at successive times in monotone order along $L$. So $\omega(x)\cap L$ has at most one point.

steps.slogan: Find a closed orbit inside the limit set.
steps.detail: Take $p\in\omega(x)$ and $q\in\omega(p)\subseteq\omega(x)$, a regular point, with a transversal $L$ at $q$. The orbit of $p$ lies in $\omega(x)$ and returns to $L$ at points tending to $q$. These points lie in $\omega(x)\cap L$, which is one point, so the orbit of $p$ meets $L$ twice at $q$ and is periodic.

steps.slogan: Show that this closed orbit is the whole limit set.
steps.detail: Let $C$ be the closed orbit. If $\omega(x)\ne C$, connectedness gives points of $\omega(x)\setminus C$ arbitrarily near some $c\in C$. In a flow box at $c$ with transversal $L$, such a point has an orbit that crosses $L$ at a point of $\omega(x)\cap L=\{c\}$, so it lies on $C$, a contradiction. Hence $\omega(x)=C$.

concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: The orbits and the flow come from the planar differential equation.

concepts.c:jordan-curve: The monotone crossing of a transversal follows from the Jordan curve theorem.

source.note: The standard proof, as in Hirsch, Smale and Devaney, Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos, chapter 10.
